thought_title: Resurrection promised through the phoenix and Scripture
orientation: The Roman church is arguing that God will raise the dead, using the phoenix as a natural sign and then quoting Scripture.
pass_a_gloss: Great and wonderful therefore we consider [it] to be, if the creator of all things resurrection will make of those who holily served him in confidence of good faith, when even through a bird he shows us the majesty of his promise? For he says somewhere: And you will raise me up, and I will confess to you, and: I lay down and slept, I woke, because you are with me. And again Job says: And you will raise up this flesh of mine which has drained all these things.

choices.why: The adverb describes the manner of serving God; 'holily' is archaic, so 'in holiness' is clearer modern English.
The phrase is a prepositional phrase with a genitive chain; 'confidence in good faith' preserves the genitive relationship without over-interpreting.
The noun refers to the greatness or magnificence of God's promise; 'majesty' fits the elevated tone.
The verb means to draw out or exhaust, often of suffering; 'drained' captures the sense of the flesh having endured or exhausted these things.

pass_b_english: Should we then consider it a great and wonderful thing that the creator of all things will raise up those who have served him in holiness, with confidence in good faith? After all, he shows us the majesty of his promise even through a bird.
For he says somewhere: “You will raise me up, and I will confess to you,” and: “I lay down and slept; I woke again, because you are with me” (Psalm 3:5).
And again Job says: “And you will raise up this flesh of mine, which has drained all these things” (Job 19:26).

problems.quote: “You will raise me up, and I will confess to you” (Psalm 16:10)
problems.source_quote: Καὶ ἐξαναστήσεις με, καὶ ἐξομολογήσομαί σοι
problems.why: The quoted Greek does not correspond to Psalm 16:10 in the LXX; the citation is incorrect.
problems.fix: Remove the Psalm 16:10 reference or replace it with the correct source for the quotation.

edits.old: “You will raise me up, and I will confess to you” (Psalm 16:10)
edits.new: “You will raise me up, and I will confess to you”

problems.quote: Should we not, then, consider it a great and wonderful thing
problems.source_quote: Μέγα καὶ θαυμαστὸν οὖν νομίζομεν εἶναι
problems.why: The Greek asks whether we find resurrection astonishing. Adding “not” and “should” makes the expected answer yes and reverses the argument.
problems.fix: Do we then consider it a great and wonderful thing if the creator of all raises those who served him in holiness, in the assurance of a good faith, when even by a bird he shows the majesty of his promise?
problems.ruling: Source is a plain statement 'Μέγα καὶ θαυμαστὸν οὖν νομίζομεν εἶναι, εἰ…' (we think it great and wonderful if…); English 'Should we not…' turns it into a rhetorical question, altering the meaning.

edits.old: Should we not, then, consider it a great and wonderful thing that
edits.new: Should we then consider it a great and wonderful thing that

fixed: negation - removed 'not': source 'Μέγα καὶ θαυμαστὸν οὖν νομίζομεν εἶναι, εἰ' asks if we find it astonishing, expecting No; 'Should we then consider...' restores that expectation.

polish.changed: Clarified the speaker of each quotation, made the rhetorical question flow naturally, and kept every claim and Scripture reference intact while smoothing the sentence rhythm for reading aloud.

last_rejected.quote: Should we not, then, consider it a great and wonderful thing that the creator of all things will raise up those who have served him in holiness, with confidence in good faith?
last_rejected.source_quote: Μέγα καὶ θαυμαστὸν οὖν νομίζομεν εἶναι, εἰ ὁ δημιουργὸς τῶν ἁπάντων ἀνάστασιν ποιήσεται τῶν ὁσίως αὐτῷ δουλευσάντων ἐν πεποιθήσει πίστεως ἀγαθῆς, …
last_rejected.why: Greek states a declarative belief; English turns it into a rhetorical question, altering modality.
last_rejected.fix: We consider it a great and wonderful thing that the creator of all things will raise up those who have served him in holiness, with confidence in good faith.
last_rejected.ruling: νομίζομεν εἶναι with εἰ can fairly render as a rhetorical question; meaning preserved.

last_rejected.quote: which has drained all these things
last_rejected.why: ἀναντλέω here means the flesh endured these sufferings, not that it drained or emptied them.
last_rejected.fix: which has endured all these things
last_rejected.ruling: ἀναντλήσασαν literally means 'drained up/drawn off'; LXX Job 19:26 uses it for flesh enduring these things. 'Drained' is a literal, defensible calque; the sense is arguably obscure but not wrong.

last_rejected.quote: Should we then consider it a great and wonderful thing that the creator of all things will raise up
last_rejected.source_quote: Μέγα καὶ θαυμαστὸν οὖν νομίζομεν εἶναι, εἰ ὁ δημιουργὸς
last_rejected.why: Source is a statement ("we think it great and wonderful", rhetorical: do we think it so?) — in effect an indicative with εἰ = "if/that". English poses it as a plain question, changing force.
last_rejected.fix: Do we then think it great and wonderful, if the creator of all things will raise up those who served him holily, with confidence of good faith, when even through a bird he shows us the greatness of his promise?
last_rejected.ruling: νομίζομεν…εἰ…; is already a rhetorical question. “Should we consider” keeps that force; “should” vs “do” is within range.
